1	# Handoff: printer and filament calibration in JusPrin
2	
3	Written 2026-10-21 for the agent who implements calibration. Nothing is coded yet; this document records the
4	decisions Kenneth made, the facts verified in OrcaSlicer's code, the design on the canvas, and the smallest build
5	that satisfies both. Read `agent-docs/jusprin/README.md` and the documents it lists first; `fork-stewardship.md`
6	governs every line you change outside `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`. This file is untracked on purpose: never commit it.
7	
8	## 1. What a calibration is, in one paragraph
9	
10	A person has a symptom (stringing, under-extrusion, bulging corners) or just wants a filament dialled in. The agent
11	decides whether a test is justified, generates OrcaSlicer's own test geometry into a project of its own, the person
12	prints it and sends a photo, the agent reads the print, and the result is saved as a new preset whose name the person
13	is told to use from now on. The product definition's section 2.11 lists the eight agent steps; this handoff is how
14	they map onto code.
15	
16	## 2. Decisions already made (Kenneth, 2026-10-21)
17	
18	1. A calibration is a project of its own, as long as the person is told what will happen before their project is
19	   closed. Not a plate in the current project (see fact 1 below for why that is impossible without rewriting Orca).
20	2. First batch: temperature tower, flow rate, pressure advance. Nothing else in this iteration.
21	3. The outcome of every test is a new preset: a named copy of the filament (or of the process or printer preset for
22	   the tests that write there). The app does not switch any project to it. The receipt names the preset and the
23	   agent tells the person to pick it from now on.
24	4. No remembered "return to the previous project". The test project is left through Home like any project.
25	5. No per-test UI. Adding a test must be a declaration plus skill text, not page code.
26	6. The physical-print ledger: "doesn't matter, whatever is the easiest". Leave it alone.
27	7. Entry points are hard-coded: a "Calibrate…" row in the project header's printer chip menu, in the filament slot
28	   menu, and in the Home printer card's kebab. A symptom typed in the project chat leads to the same flow.
29	
30	## 3. Facts verified in the code (read, not run)
31	
32	1. **Every OrcaSlicer generator replaces the open project and edits project-wide presets.** `Plater::calib_pa`,
33	   `calib_temp`, `calib_flowrate`, `calib_max_vol_speed`, `calib_retraction`, `calib_VFA`, the input-shaping pair and
34	   `Calib_Cornering` (`src/slic3r/GUI/Plater.cpp` from about line 12677) each call `new_project()` and then write to
35	   `preset_bundle->prints/filaments/printers.get_edited_preset().config`. Plates have no presets of their own, so a
36	   test on a plate of an existing project would change every other plate. Do not try.
37	2. **The test's parameters are runtime-only.** The generator stores them on the current plate's `Print` with
38	   `set_calib_params` (`Print.hpp:1089`); `GCode.cpp` reads them per layer (temperature at line 4697). Nothing writes
39	   them to the 3MF, and loading a project resets the mode to none at `Plater.cpp:5891`. A saved temperature tower,
40	   reopened, slices as a plain tower at one temperature. The pressure-advance pattern is the exception: its per-layer
41	   commands go into the plate's custom G-code, which the 3MF does save. The PA pattern also hard-codes the first
42	   plate's origin (`Plater.cpp:12814`).
43	3. **OrcaSlicer already treats one outcome as a new preset.** The Bambu wizard's save page writes flow results as a
44	   filament preset named "<filament> Flow Rate Calibrated" (`CalibrationWizardSavePage.cpp:37`). Its pressure-advance
45	   results go to the machine, not a preset. The SoftFever dialogs (`calib_dlg.cpp`) save nothing: the person types
46	   the value into a preset by hand.
47	4. **Saving a copy already exists and selects the copy.** `settings_apply_patch` with `persistAs` saves through
48	   Orca's own `Tab::save_preset` and asserts the copy is now selected
49	   (`Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:3356-3369`); the result carries `saved_as`. A stock preset cannot be
50	   overwritten and the preview says so with `read_only_preset` and a suggested copy name (`check_persist`, line
51	   2941). Whether a process-scope copy works end to end is unverified; filament and printer are in use today.
52	5. **Which preset each result belongs to** (from `Preset.cpp`'s option lists): nozzle temperature, flow ratio,
53	   pressure advance, retraction length (as a filament override) and max volumetric speed are filament settings; VFA
54	   writes wall speeds in the process preset; cornering writes junction deviation (process) or jerk limits (printer);
55	   input shaping and Bambu's measured pressure advance live on the machine and produce no preset.
56	6. **The skill mechanism is ready.** `AgentUI/src/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with a `description:` in its frontmatter is
57	   listed to the model and read on demand through the `skill_read` tool (`Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp:1209`,
58	   `AgentHost.cpp:2467`). The four skills that exist today are all trigger-based, so this would be the first
59	   on-demand one. Text limit 16 KiB; one skill per directory; name equals directory name (`skillParser.ts`).
60	7. **The project-replacing path already exists.** The `project_open` tool saves the open project to its version
61	   history, drops unsaved preset edits, and calls `m_plater.new_project(true, true, name)` with confirmations skipped
62	   (`OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:2450-2467`, `ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:1005`). The generate tool should take the
63	   same route, not a second one.
64	8. **The setup card is already data-driven.** `setup_record` (`ToolRegistry.cpp:1071`) titles the pinned card from a
65	   purpose and headline. A calibration project needs no new pinned card: the agent records the test as the purpose
66	   and the range as the headline.
67	
68	## 4. The design
69	
70	JusPrin v2 canvas, page "Calibration · Printer & Filament": https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v
71	(nine boards, `calibration-01…08` plus `05b`). The builder that drew them is outside the repo at
72	`~/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/figma-mirror/tools/composer/build_calibration_page.py`.
73	
74	- Board 1: the three "Calibrate…" rows.
75	- Board 2: a symptom in the project chat. The agent explains, then says in its own words that the current project
76	  will be saved and closed, that the test's settings are temporary, and that nothing is written until the person
77	  chooses. The reply choice is the confirmation.
78	- Board 3: the dialog the menu path shows, carrying the same two facts, because no agent sentence precedes it.
79	- Board 4: the test project. Pinned card from `setup_record`; the agent's first message says what to print and what
80	  to photograph; "Change the range" is the manual control.
81	- Board 5 and 5b: the photo comes back, the agent names the block and why, and proposes one write through the
82	  ordinary settings preview rows plus the preset it is saved as. 5b shows the card is one shape with slots (value,
83	  scope, base preset and printer, setting old → new, the word for what the person picks) and three instances.
84	- Board 6: the receipt with Undo. The agent tells the person the preset name to pick from now on; nothing switches.
85	- Board 7: the test reopened later warns that the steps are not in the file and offers to regenerate.
86	- Board 8: the test on Home as an ordinary project whose status line names the preset it produced.
87	
88	The strings on the boards are illustrations; the agent writes its own. Keep the two facts of board 2 and 3 verbatim
89	in meaning: the project closes, the test's edits are temporary.
90	
91	## 5. The build: one tool, one skill, three rows, one optional seam
92	
93	Do not build: a `calibration_list` tool (the tests are static knowledge; the workspace already reports printer,
94	filament and nozzle), per-test cards, a return hook, preset switching, or Bambu's automatic path. Correct the tool
95	guide (`agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md`, the `calibration` table around line 561): the
96	`calibration_generate` row says "onto a new plate", which fact 1 rules out, and `calibration_list` is dropped.
97	
98	### 5.1 The tool: `calibration_generate`
99	
100	One registered tool (`Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp`, handler in `ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp`, adapter work in
101	`Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp`). Input: `test` (`temperature`, `flow`, `pressure_advance` for now), the
102	test's parameters as Orca's dialogs take them (temperature and pressure advance: `start`, `end`, `step`; pressure
103	advance also `method` line/pattern/tower and `extruderType`; flow: `pass` 1 or 2 and `linear`), and `projectName`.
104	It runs the same release-and-replace sequence as `project_open` (fact 7), then calls the matching `Plater::calib_*`
105	with a `Calib_Params`. Output: the new project's name, the plate and object ids, and the parameters as applied
106	(Orca clamps and substitutes; return what it did). Classify it as a mutation that replaces the project, with the
107	same session-invalidation the open tool has. Mark it in-app only until the MCP side is wanted.
108	
109	The generators call `new_project(false, false, name)` themselves, with confirmations on. Either skip the generator's
110	own call by releasing the project first through the open path and accepting the generator's then-trivial
111	`new_project`, or add a small product-neutral seam so the generator can be told the project is already fresh.
112	Prefer the first; measure before adding a seam. Whatever you do, the version-history save must happen before any
113	preset edit, or the person's project loses its unsaved preset changes.
114	
115	### 5.2 The skill: `AgentUI/src/skills/calibration/SKILL.md`
116	
117	Frontmatter: `name: calibration`, `description:` one line that makes the model read it when a print symptom points
118	at the material or when the person asks to calibrate. Body, in sections:
119	
120	1. When a test is justified, and which symptoms point to which test (stringing and hairs: temperature first,
121	   retraction second; under-extrusion, gaps, bulging corners or top surface: flow; corner bulges and gap at seams at
122	   speed: pressure advance). Say when drying the spool or checking the nozzle comes first.
123	2. Before generating: say the two facts (project saved and closed; temporary settings) and get a reply. From a menu
124	   entry the app has already asked; from a symptom the agent asks.
125	3. Per test: the default range per material, taken from OrcaSlicer's own dialog defaults (`calib_dlg.cpp` has the
126	   PLA, ABS/ASA, PETG, PCTG, TPU, PA-CF, PET-CF sets for temperature); what the person should photograph; how to
127	   read the print; which setting the result writes and in which preset scope; how to name the copy.
128	4. After generating: call `setup_record` with the test as the purpose and the range as the headline, then tell the
129	   person to slice and print and what to photograph.
130	5. Reading the photo: name the best block or tile and why, name the runner-up, and propose one write with
131	   `settings_preview_patch` then `settings_apply_patch` with `persistAs`. Naming rule: "<base> · <printer>
132	   calibrated"; a second test on the same base writes into that copy, never a second name. If the person is already
133	   on their own non-stock preset, writing in place with no new name is an option Kenneth has not ruled on: ask in
134	   the handover, do not decide it in the skill.
135	6. After saving: say the preset's name, that this test uses it now, that other projects keep their filament until
136	   the person picks it, and offer the next test without starting it.
137	7. A reopened test: the steps are not in the file (fact 2); regenerate before slicing again.
138	
139	Keep conversation rules in the skill and one-tool rules in the tool description (`rule-lives-next-to-what-it-governs`
140	in memory). Add one line to `skills/print-issues/SKILL.md` pointing at this skill for material symptoms.
141	
142	### 5.3 The entry rows
143	
144	- Project header, printer chip: `Shell/PrinterMenu.cpp` beside "Printer settings…" (about line 176).
145	- Project header, filament slot sub-list: `Shell/FilamentMenu.cpp` beside "Filament settings…" (about line 461).
146	- Home card kebab: `HomeUI/src/components/PrinterMenu.tsx`, the action through `Home/HomeHost.cpp` and
147	  `Home/OrcaHomeBackend.cpp` like `open_printer_settings`.
148	
149	A row opens the project chat (the agent pane, not the printer panel: the test needs the project tools) with the
150	confirmation dialog of board 3 first, then a message the person is shown as their own, such as "Calibrate the
151	temperature for Gray PETG on Prusa MK4", so the skill takes over. Use Orca's `MessageDialog`, never
152	`wxMessageBox` (memory: `use-orca-messagedialog`). Every colour and size comes from `ShellTheme` and the tokens.
153	
154	### 5.4 Optional seam: keep the test valid after a reload
155	
156	Fact 2 means a reopened test is a plain tower. Two ways out, pick after measuring: (a) a workspace fact
157	`calibration.generatedThisSession` the skill reads, plus board 7's regenerate offer; or (b) store the `Calib_Params`
158	with the fork's own project data (`Agent/ProjectPersistence`) and re-apply `set_calib_params` on the plate's print
159	after load. (b) removes board 7's warning entirely and is small if the load observer in `Workspace/FileLoads` can
160	run it; the preset edits already come back with the project. The PA pattern's custom G-code needs nothing.
161	
162	## 6. Verification required before calling it done
163	
164	- Adapter test (Catch2, `tests/workspace`): generate each of the three tests from a project with unsaved preset
165	  edits; assert a version was saved first, the new project is named, the plate holds the test objects, and the
166	  print's `calib_params` match the request. Then reload the saved test and assert what fact 2 says, or what seam
167	  (b) fixes.
168	- Settings test: a preview with `persistAs` on a stock filament reports `read_only_preset` with the copy name;
169	  apply with the copy name saves and selects it; a second apply with the same copy name updates it (no second copy).
170	- Page tests (Vitest): the skill parses, is listed with its description, and stays under the size limit.
171	- Prompt tests, like `tests/printer_prompt` and `tests/project_prompt`: a symptom message leads to the two facts
172	  and a reply choice before any generate call; a photo turn leads to exactly one preview and one apply with the
173	  naming rule. Record requests with the shell harness; no live-model batch without Kenneth approving it (memory:
174	  `prompt-eval-spend-budget`).
175	- One shell-harness run with `--manual-mcp` driving `calibration_generate` and the settings tools end to end on the
176	  fake Bambu printer (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md`).
177	- The three rows open the chat and show the dialog; the dialog's Cancel leaves the project untouched.
178	
179	## 7. Open questions for Kenneth
180	
181	1. Write in place when the person is already on their own preset, or always a named copy?
182	2. Should the generate tool be offered over MCP in this iteration, or in-app only?
183	3. Seam (a) or (b) in 5.4, once you have measured (b).
184	
185	## 8. Pointers
186	
187	- Product definition 2.11, 3.3 and 4.2: `agent-docs/jusprin/product-definition.md`.
188	- Tool and skill rules: `agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md`, sections "Decide whether this should be a

When fixing one visible failure (e.g. a system-prompt bug in one conversation mode), Kenneth expects the fix to be judged against every related scenario, not just the reported one. He said (2026-09-28) that I tend to solve the problem in front of me and break "a lot more situations" that aren't in view, and asked me to research best practice online instead of reasoning from the one bug.

**Why:** On the printer-panel prompt this was borne out: a two-line fix for the Change conversation silently took Add-mode `add-not-now-done` from 19/20 to 3/20; only a side-by-side full-suite run caught it.

**How to apply:**
- Before editing a shared prompt/component, build or extend a test set covering all its scenarios (off-script inputs, regressions from git history), then compare old vs new in the same run (`tests/printer_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py --prompt-rev HEAD`).
- Scope a fix to the scenario it's for; keep measured wording for the others byte-identical.
- Don't let the current bug drive general recommendations — look for external best practice first.

On 2026-10-14, after a long run of experiment reports on the project assistant's prompt, Kenneth said: "You have to restate everything in plain English, it's very difficult to read your text."

The reports he was reacting to were packed with tool names, arm names, "3 of 3" counts, tables and compressed bullet labels.

**Why:** he reads these to decide what to do next, often quickly, and he judges results by whether the explanation makes sense in the real world ("the rubber has to meet the road"), not by the numbers from a small test set. He said the same day that with small samples "we cannot just look at the numbers... we need to use common sense to see if the attribution makes sense."

**How to apply:** (my interpretation) write to him in ordinary sentences. Say what happened and why it makes sense, as you would to someone who was not watching. Keep code identifiers, arm names and counts to the few that carry the point, and explain a term the first time it appears. Lead with the answer. Prefer a short explanation of cause over a table of outcomes. When passing work to sub-agents, tell them the same: judge by whether the cause is believable, and check results against how the product is really used. See [[fix-without-breaking-other-scenarios]].

# Guide for adding JusPrin tools

**Status:** This guide explains how to add a tool to JusPrin. The three things it builds on are already implemented: the shared tool registry, the MCP server embedded in the app, and the stdio bridge (a small helper program that connects external AI clients to that server). Over MCP, the tools currently cover inspecting the workspace, reporting on a slice for review, and the settings workflow. The settings workflow works on the process preset, on one object, and on filament and printer presets. Later in this guide there is a [candidate catalog](#candidate-catalog): a list of tools we might build, worked out from the product's screens. It follows the implemented catalog record. Nothing in the candidate catalog exists unless the catalog record says it does.

JusPrin has one tool system. A new capability is defined once, in the shared registry. `ToolExecutionCoordinator` runs it. Its implementation reads and changes the open project through the typed workspace interface. Two adapters, one for OpenAI and one for MCP, only translate that single definition into the format each side expects. The aim of this guide is a tool catalog that stays small, does only what it claims to do, can change safely over time, and is shaped by real printing tasks. It should not be shaped by a list of every feature OrcaSlicer has.

Treat this guide as the starting point. Change it when what you learn from implementing, from real MCP clients, or from evals shows that a rule, a contract, a limit, or a sequence here should change. Do not keep a planning assumption just because it is written here. Base every revision on evidence, and describe significant changes in the PR. Two things do not change: OrcaSlicer stays the owner of the state it owns, and the verification requirements stay.

Before you touch any OrcaSlicer class that holds live state, read [the production documentation](README.md), [production architecture](architecture.md), and [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md). The current tool definitions are in [`ToolRegistry.cpp`](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp). The code that runs them is in [`ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp`](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp). The code that presents them over MCP is in [`McpProtocol.cpp`](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp).

External clients on the same machine connect through the bundled `jusprin-mcp` stdio helper, which is set up from **Connect AI tools...**. The helper and the server inside the app are compiled from the same registry. So every new tool you offer must have the same catalog entry and the same schema whether the app is running (live) or not (offline), for the same build and the same negotiated protocol version. Do not add a catalog that exists in only one adapter. Connecting to the server directly over HTTP is a route for developers. It is not what the default setup instructions tell people to do.

## Words this guide uses

- **Registry.** The one list of tool definitions, compiled into the app (`ToolRegistry.cpp`).
- **Catalog.** The list of tools as a caller sees it.
- **Coordinator.** `ToolExecutionCoordinator`, the class that queues tool calls and runs them on the GUI thread.
- **Workspace.** The typed C++ interface (`IWorkspace`) through which JusPrin reads and changes the open project. It has two implementations, called workspace adapters. The real one works on live OrcaSlicer. The fake one is for tests.
- **Tool adapter.** Code that translates registry definitions and results for one kind of caller. There are two: the in-app adapter, which uses OpenAI's format and serves the Agent panel, and the MCP adapter, which serves external clients. "Both adapters" in this guide means these two.
- **Projection.** The form in which one tool adapter presents a definition or a result.
- **Exposure.** The registry setting that says which callers are offered a tool.
- **Owner.** The OrcaSlicer class that holds the real copy of some state, or that already implements an operation.
- **Seam.** A small addition to a file OrcaSlicer owns, which lets fork code call or observe OrcaSlicer's behavior.
- **Session and revision.** `sessionId` identifies the project that is currently open. `revision` is a counter the workspace raises when its state changes. A call that was prepared against an older session or revision is called stale.
- **Action class.** Whether a tool is read-only, a mutation (it changes something), or destructive.
- **Dirty.** A preset is dirty when it has unsaved edits.
- **Eval.** An automated test that gives a model a task and checks the transcript that results.
- **M0 to M5.** The milestones in which the tool catalog was delivered.

## Current connection and execution boundary

- The server starts automatically with the JusPrin Agent panel. There is no `JUSPRIN_MCP` switch to enable it and no bearer token. The server listens only on the numeric loopback address. It prefers port 47301, and falls back to a port chosen by the operating system only when 47301 is taken.
- The shell tells the server where its discovery file is: `<data_dir>/jusprin/mcp.json`. The running server writes its details there in one atomic step: the actual address, the PID, a unique `instanceId` for this run, the build version, and the protocol versions. Before a server removes the record, it checks, while holding the discovery lock, that the record is its own. An older server therefore cannot remove a newer server's record, even inside the same process. On POSIX systems the file has mode `0600`.
- The helper checks that the discovery file is valid, and then tests that the address in it answers. When the app starts or restarts later, the helper follows the new record. The helper never launches JusPrin. The discovery file holds one record, and the last server to write it wins. So the helper works with one selected instance; there is no way to choose among several. `--discovery`, `JUSPRIN_MCP_DISCOVERY`, and `JUSPRIN_MCP_URL` override the file path or the address. They do not switch anything on. The connection entries that Connect writes use `--discovery` with the app's actual data directory.
- When the app is not running, the helper answers discovery and tool-list requests from the registry compiled into the helper. Tool calls made while the app is not running return `workspace_unavailable`. When the app can be reached, the helper uses the app's live catalog and results, even when the app and the helper are different versions. Do not replace a live app's tool list with the helper's compiled one. A version difference between the two is logged.
- The HTTP adapter accepts MCP protocol version `2026-07-28`. The helper can also negotiate the older versions `2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25`. The helper does all conversion between versions. Code that executes a tool must not behave differently for different protocol versions.
- **Connect** shows the person the command or the file edit and asks for confirmation first. Then it either runs the Claude Code or Codex CLI, or merges the JusPrin entry into the JSON configuration of Claude Desktop/local Cowork, Cursor or VS Code. A JSON edit keeps unrelated settings and makes a backup. It is refused when the preview is out of date or when the destination is a symlink. It does not protect against another editor writing the same file at the exact moment of replacement.
- On macOS the helper is bundled next to the app executable. Windows has a matching install rule. On Linux, the entry for an AppImage uses the installed image's path plus `--mcp-bridge`, and the app handles that flag before the GUI starts. Do not save a temporary AppImage mount path as the command.

Workspace commands run on the GUI thread, through the shared coordinator. A timer owned by the shell keeps execution moving, so execution does not depend on the WebView's handshake. No external client ever gets direct access to OrcaSlicer objects.

A call from an external client is tagged `ToolSource::Mcp`. The MCP adapter sets that tag, so it can be trusted, and it is kept for the activity history and for diagnostics. External calls run through the same coordinator and the same workspace commands as calls from the in-app Agent. The change log records the edits they make, as it records every edit, and marks them `external`. In the conversation thread those edits appear as rows that say "External tool", where a change made in the app says "Agent".

## Start with an eval failure

The fact that OrcaSlicer has a menu item or a config key is not a reason to add a tool. Start from a transcript or an automated eval in which the Agent cannot finish a real user task, finishes it only some of the time, or needs an unreasonable number of steps or tokens.

Write down:

- what the user wanted to achieve;
- the exact point where the current tools stop being enough;
- which OrcaSlicer state or operation is missing;
- what a successful transcript should look like;
- the unsafe or ambiguous cases that must fail; and
- the evidence that will show the new tool fixed the problem.

If the failure can be fixed by a clearer description, a better result, or a more useful validation error, improve the existing definition instead of adding a tool.

The candidate catalog later in this guide lists tools we might build. Being listed there does not accept a tool, and it does not excuse a tool from this section. A row in that catalog does two jobs. It records which product screen and which group of evals the tool would serve, which makes the eval easier to write. It also settles what the tool acts on, its action class, and its OrcaSlicer owner, so that two people do not build the same capability twice under different names.

## Decide whether this should be a tool

Add or extend a tool when the Agent needs one of three things: up-to-date state read straight from OrcaSlicer, a calculation that OrcaSlicer does and that always gives the same answer for the same input, or a change to the live project.

Do not add a tool for:

- a single setting key. Setting keys are records that the generic settings tools search and edit;
- general printing advice that the model can work out from a skill;
- a fixed bundle of changes such as "make it stronger", where the right answer depends on the part and on what the user cares about;
- driving the UI, such as pressing a button or operating a widget or a hidden panel;
- data that an existing tool already returns in a size-limited result;
- a capability someone might want in the future, with no eval or user task behind it; or
- an operation that the real workspace adapter cannot truly perform through the OrcaSlicer class that owns it.

A fixed, mechanical step of a workflow can be a tool. Examples are generating OrcaSlicer's calibration geometry and starting OrcaSlicer's slice action. Advice should stay a skill until there is a separately specified operation behind it that always behaves the same way.

## Skills versus tools

A skill is text the model reads. A tool is something the app executes. To decide which one a candidate is, ask one question: does it have to run, or does it only have to be read?

- It has to run if it reads state the model does not have, computes something only OrcaSlicer can compute, or changes the project. That makes it a tool.
- It only has to be read if it is judgement, the order to do things in, facts about printing, how to interpret a tool's result, or which question to ask first. That makes it a skill.

The section above covers tools. This section covers skills, and decides the cases that fall in between.

A skill contains things the model could do by itself if it had the right knowledge. It contains nothing that executes. Examples:

- judging evidence, such as telling an adhesion failure from wet filament in a photo;
- the order of a series of tool calls, and the reasons for that order. For "make it stronger": read the settings, change walls and infill, slice, read the report;
- facts about printing, such as what PETG tolerates;
- which question to ask when the answer would change the plan.

A skill is a file on the Agent page, `AgentUI/src/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: frontmatter with its `name` and a `trigger`, a `description` or both, then the text the model gets. The page sends every skill once per connection with the `skills` bridge message. A skill with a trigger is the app's: when the event it names happens, the host adds it to the one request where the model first reads about the event, as the request's last item, and to no later request. A skill with a description is the model's: `skill_read` lists the described skills in its own description and returns one by name, and is offered only while at least one exists (none does yet). Four skills have triggers, one file each:

- `file-loaded` (trigger `file_loaded`): the first message after a file is opened or imported is a judgement about the load report. It fires when the person opens or drops a file, after an in-app `object_import` (and a failed `project_open`) in the same turn, and in the opened project's chat after an in-app `project_open`, which replaces the conversation and so ends the turn that asked. An MCP client's loads fire nothing. The host sends a picture of the active plate with it and, when no purpose is recorded, one sentence of its own built from that state.
- `project-setup-changed` (trigger `setup_changed`): check the setup in force against the print's purpose. It fires on the result of an in-app `setup_record` that recorded a purpose for the first time or changed its fields (its result says which in `purposeChange`; a call that only restates the title to change the plan does not fire it), when the printer, filament, process or plate type differs from the setup the model was last asked to check under a recorded purpose (on the next tool result of the turn, or on the next turn's first request when the person changed it by hand), and on a turn's first request after the person restored an earlier version while a purpose is recorded. Each time the model is asked to check, the app saves the setup in force as the one checked. The model's own successful `printer_setup` fires nothing: the setup it chose is saved as checked at once (Kenneth, 2026-10-19), so the skill is for a setup that moved without the model, and a pairing its change breaks is caught by the slice-refusal facts and skill. It gives way to the file-loaded skill on a request that carries both, since that skill already asks for the same check.
- `slice-failed` (trigger `slice_failed`): a plate's last slice did not succeed, because OrcaSlicer's check refused the plate or the run failed. The adapter records why on the plate (`WorkspacePlate::slice_failure`: refused or failed, OrcaSlicer's words, the setting and object when named) at the moment it happens (a hook in `Plater::reslice`, `Workspace/SliceRequests.hpp`, and the run's completion event), worded by the print-issue monitor's `slice_failure_of`, and keeps it until the plate slices. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceFailure`; `slice_report` of an unsliced plate adds the check code and the object's name. The skill fires once per failure, on the first request that carries it: the result of the model's own `slice_start`, the turn the app starts when a slice the model started fails after its turn, or the next message after the person's Slice all. The same refusal again is the same failure.
- `print-issues` (trigger `print_issues`): what the print-issue chip's two buttons ask for and how to read what OrcaSlicer reports. The adapter reads a slice's warnings through the monitor's `slice_warnings_of` while the plate is active and keeps a summary on the plate while that slice is current (`WorkspacePlate::slice_warnings`: the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning, critical first, in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object). It counts every warning the chip lists, so the bed-temperature warning too, which `slice_report` leaves out. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceWarnings`. The skill fires on the request that carries a chip's message, and on the first request whose workspace shows warnings no request has carried yet, whether the person sliced (their next message) or the model did (the tool result that shows them, or the app's turn when its slice ended after its turn); a re-slice with the same warnings fires nothing.

The cases in between:

- **A procedure made of existing tool calls.** It is a skill for as long as carrying it out takes judgement. It becomes a tool only when the steps are fixed and the person wants the whole thing as one action that can be undone. If there are many such fixed sequences, they go in one workflow registry (see [When resources or skills are appropriate](#when-resources-or-skills-are-appropriate)).
- **An analysis.** It is a tool when OrcaSlicer computes it and always gets the same answer, such as overhang angles from geometry. It is a skill when it is a judgement about evidence. Pair that skill with the tool that supplies the evidence (`view_render`, `slice_report`).
- **Large reference data.** When the model needs only one part of the data, make it a tool that returns the part an argument selects, as `settings_search` does. When the model needs to see all of the data before it can use any of it, make it text. The printer list described under [Input design](#input-design) is the case we measured: putting the whole list in the instructions worked better than the search tool.
- **A tool description versus a skill.** A tool description says when to call that one tool, in the words a person would use. A skill says how several tools fit together and what to conclude from their results. If a tool description has grown into a step-by-step procedure, move the procedure out into a skill.

When you are not sure, start with a skill. A skill is a text file that ships with the page. A tool costs the whole implementation sequence described below, including fakes, tests, and rebase evidence. Turn a skill into a tool only on the kind of evidence every tool starts from (see [Start with an eval failure](#start-with-an-eval-failure)). Either transcripts show the model getting the sequence wrong in ways that better text does not fix, or the action needs something only the app can give: all-or-nothing application, validation, or undo. The opposite sign exists too. If a skill has turned into exact values and calls in a fixed order, with no judgement between them, it should be written as a tool.

How something gets loaded into the model's context does not decide whether it is a skill or a tool. Today a skill costs its one line in the instructions, and a tool costs its definition on the first request of a conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). If we later use the model platform's deferred loading, both will cost one index line plus a load when needed. A skill could then be a deferred read-only tool: the tool's description is the skill's index line, and the tool's result is the skill's text. Tools and skills would then be found the same way and covered by the same eval.

## Read, mutation, and destructive policy

Decide what a tool may do from its action class in the registry, not from its name:

- **Read-only:** cannot change the project, a preset, anything on disk, the printer, or any product state that is saved.
- **Mutation:** changes the project, a preset, or saved product state.
- **Destructive:** may delete, overwrite, discard, print, export, or restore history.

The action class is information used for UI wording, MCP annotations, staleness checks, and the audit history. A valid tool call starts as soon as it has been validated. A tool that previews changes counts as read-only only if tests against both the fake and the real workspace adapter prove that it does none of these: make a preset dirty, raise the workspace revision, create history, cancel slicing, or write a file.

## Asynchronous operations

Make a tool asynchronous only when the real OrcaSlicer operation is asynchronous. Do not build a second engine for running jobs.

Slicing, and any long-running action added later, works like this:

1. The workspace command starts the work through its current OrcaSlicer owner and returns a stable action handle.
2. `ToolActivity` records that the action is running, and then its final state, with a limited amount of progress information.
3. When OrcaSlicer completes or fails, the workspace state advances or is invalidated.
4. After that event, the caller fetches the real slice report or the error.
5. Cancelling calls OrcaSlicer's real cancellation path, and reports whether the cancellation took effect before the work finished.

MCP progress notifications are optional. They belong to one request and exist only to show progress. The progress value must never go backwards, and a client must always have another way to learn the final result. Add the MCP Tasks extension only when a real client or eval needs durable calls that outlive one request. An operation taking several seconds is not enough reason.

The current coordinator runs an action in steps, on GUI ticks. It does not provide durable asynchronous jobs. The bridge accepts `notifications/cancelled` in both the legacy and the modern protocol versions. On receiving one, it closes the connection it was forwarding and suppresses any further output for that request. End of input (EOF) ends the bridge session. If the connection is lost before the final response, the client gets `connection_lost` with an **unknown outcome** warning. That is not proof that the mutation was cancelled. Never retry a mutation automatically after such a loss. Read the real state first.

## Tool exposure

By default, offer a tool through both adapters when both can supply the same inputs. Offer it through only one when the two sides get their context in different ways. The current cases:

- `workspace_inspect` is offered through both adapters. Either side can then get the identity of a newly completed slice after slicing, without relying on the context it was given at the start of the turn.
- Import from an attachment (`object_import`) is in-app only, and import from a path (`object_import_file`) is MCP only. In the first case the file reaches the app through the conversation. In the second it arrives as an explicit path. These are two separate definitions that each say exactly what they do, both built on one workspace command. They are not one tool that behaves differently for different callers.
- `setup_record` is in-app only. The intent record and the pinned plan belong to the in-app chat. An external agent keeps what its user said, and its own plan, in its own conversation. MCP clients can still read both through `workspace_inspect` and `slice_report`. For the same reason, the in-app assistant's print guidance, which names these tools, is not part of the MCP server's instructions. That guidance is the "Intent and setup", "Preparation" and "Verification" paragraphs of the in-app prompt, written on the page in `AgentUI/src/projectInstructions.ts`.
- A future MCP diagnostics tool may be MCP only, if its purpose is to establish the external connection.
- The printer panel's five own tools carry only the `Printer` exposure. Neither adapter lists them. The panel's conversation offers all of them in every mode and refuses the calls that do not fit the conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). What the model reads back from one of these tools is the tool's own result. It is not wrapped in the host's workspace envelope.

Write the reason for a restricted exposure next to the registry definition, and test it. Do not use exposure to make one tool behave differently for different callers. If two adapters need different behavior, either improve the shared command or create two separate definitions that each say what they really do.

## When resources or skills are appropriate

Do not make anything depend on MCP resources until the clients we intend to support have shown that their models fetch resources reliably. A tool that returns a size-limited amount of data is what every client can be expected to handle. Resources may be added as an optional second way to get data that is large, readable, and stable.

Keep printing playbooks as skills the model can read (see [Skills versus tools](#skills-versus-tools)). Examples are reducing stringing, improving strength, and choosing a support strategy. Turn a workflow into an executable tool only when it corresponds to a named OrcaSlicer operation that always behaves the same way and has defined inputs, outputs, validation, and behavior for undo, reset, and cancellation. If many step-by-step workflows eventually qualify, build one workflow registry that the model can search, in preference to dozens of nearly identical tool definitions.

## Required implementation sequence for one new tool

1. Add or update the failing eval and the expected transcript.
2. Find the real OrcaSlicer owner. Record how it behaves: object lifetimes, threading, undo history, and events.
3. Define the typed inputs, outputs, and errors of the workspace command.
4. Implement the command in the fake workspace adapter, and write the workspace contract tests.
5. Implement the command in the real workspace adapter, through the smallest possible seam in the owner.
6. Prove that making the edit directly in the GUI and making it through the tool leave the same observable state.
7. Add the registry definition, the decoder and validator, the link to the code that executes the tool, and the output schema.
8. Add coordinator tests for action class, staleness, all-or-nothing behavior, cancellation, and the final activity state.
9. Add projection tests for every adapter that offers the tool.
10. Add protocol fixtures and output-limit tests.
11. Run a harness against the real app, and record one end-to-end transcript with an external client.
12. Update the catalog below, and attach the verification and rebase evidence to the PR.

Do not merge a registry entry that is backed only by the fake workspace.

## Test matrix

Every new capability needs tests at each layer it passes through:

| Layer | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Registry | unique name, deterministic ordering, valid schemas, correct exposure and action class |
| Decoder | valid inputs, unknown fields, type errors, bounds, conflicting selectors |
| Fake workspace | success, expected failures, revision, events, atomicity, native undo/reset/revert and cancel semantics |
| Coordinator | stale session/revision, cancellation race, terminal result |
| Real adapter | live Orca owner, GUI parity, truthful undo/reset/revert behavior, slicing invalidation/completion, document replacement |
| OpenAI adapter | canonical schema projection and successful continuation |
| MCP adapter | canonical schema/output projection, bounded response, protocol errors, disconnect behavior |
| Shell/eval | real project and intended client complete the user task |

If a layer does not apply, say why in the PR. If something cannot be tested, state that openly as a limitation. It is not permission to leave out evidence without saying so.

32	- The server starts automatically with the JusPrin Agent panel. There is no `JUSPRIN_MCP` switch to enable it and no bearer token. The server listens only on the numeric loopback address. It prefers port 47301, and falls back to a port chosen by the operating system only when 47301 is taken.
33	- The shell tells the server where its discovery file is: `<data_dir>/jusprin/mcp.json`. The running server writes its details there in one atomic step: the actual address, the PID, a unique `instanceId` for this run, the build version, and the protocol versions. Before a server removes the record, it checks, while holding the discovery lock, that the record is its own. An older server therefore cannot remove a newer server's record, even inside the same process. On POSIX systems the file has mode `0600`.
34	- The helper checks that the discovery file is valid, and then tests that the address in it answers. When the app starts or restarts later, the helper follows the new record. The helper never launches JusPrin. The discovery file holds one record, and the last server to write it wins. So the helper works with one selected instance; there is no way to choose among several. `--discovery`, `JUSPRIN_MCP_DISCOVERY`, and `JUSPRIN_MCP_URL` override the file path or the address. They do not switch anything on. The connection entries that Connect writes use `--discovery` with the app's actual data directory.
35	- When the app is not running, the helper answers discovery and tool-list requests from the registry compiled into the helper. Tool calls made while the app is not running return `workspace_unavailable`. When the app can be reached, the helper uses the app's live catalog and results, even when the app and the helper are different versions. Do not replace a live app's tool list with the helper's compiled one. A version difference between the two is logged.
36	- The HTTP adapter accepts MCP protocol version `2026-07-28`. The helper can also negotiate the older versions `2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25`. The helper does all conversion between versions. Code that executes a tool must not behave differently for different protocol versions.
37	- **Connect** shows the person the command or the file edit and asks for confirmation first. Then it either runs the Claude Code or Codex CLI, or merges the JusPrin entry into the JSON configuration of Claude Desktop/local Cowork, Cursor or VS Code. A JSON edit keeps unrelated settings and makes a backup. It is refused when the preview is out of date or when the destination is a symlink. It does not protect against another editor writing the same file at the exact moment of replacement.
38	- On macOS the helper is bundled next to the app executable. Windows has a matching install rule. On Linux, the entry for an AppImage uses the installed image's path plus `--mcp-bridge`, and the app handles that flag before the GUI starts. Do not save a temporary AppImage mount path as the command.
39	
40	Workspace commands run on the GUI thread, through the shared coordinator. A timer owned by the shell keeps execution moving, so execution does not depend on the WebView's handshake. No external client ever gets direct access to OrcaSlicer objects.
41	
42	A call from an external client is tagged `ToolSource::Mcp`. The MCP adapter sets that tag, so it can be trusted, and it is kept for the activity history and for diagnostics. External calls run through the same coordinator and the same workspace commands as calls from the in-app Agent. The change log records the edits they make, as it records every edit, and marks them `external`. In the conversation thread those edits appear as rows that say "External tool", where a change made in the app says "Agent".

44	## Start with an eval failure
45	
46	The fact that OrcaSlicer has a menu item or a config key is not a reason to add a tool. Start from a transcript or an automated eval in which the Agent cannot finish a real user task, finishes it only some of the time, or needs an unreasonable number of steps or tokens.
47	
48	Write down:
49	
50	- what the user wanted to achieve;
51	- the exact point where the current tools stop being enough;
52	- which OrcaSlicer state or operation is missing;
53	- what a successful transcript should look like;
54	- the unsafe or ambiguous cases that must fail; and
55	- the evidence that will show the new tool fixed the problem.
56	
57	If the failure can be fixed by a clearer description, a better result, or a more useful validation error, improve the existing definition instead of adding a tool.
58	
59	The candidate catalog later in this guide lists tools we might build. Being listed there does not accept a tool, and it does not excuse a tool from this section. A row in that catalog does two jobs. It records which product screen and which group of evals the tool would serve, which makes the eval easier to write. It also settles what the tool acts on, its action class, and its OrcaSlicer owner, so that two people do not build the same capability twice under different names.
60	
61	## Decide whether this should be a tool
62	
63	Add or extend a tool when the Agent needs one of three things: up-to-date state read straight from OrcaSlicer, a calculation that OrcaSlicer does and that always gives the same answer for the same input, or a change to the live project.
64	
65	Do not add a tool for:
66	
67	- a single setting key. Setting keys are records that the generic settings tools search and edit;
68	- general printing advice that the model can work out from a skill;
69	- a fixed bundle of changes such as "make it stronger", where the right answer depends on the part and on what the user cares about;
70	- driving the UI, such as pressing a button or operating a widget or a hidden panel;
71	- data that an existing tool already returns in a size-limited result;
72	- a capability someone might want in the future, with no eval or user task behind it; or
73	- an operation that the real workspace adapter cannot truly perform through the OrcaSlicer class that owns it.
74	
75	A fixed, mechanical step of a workflow can be a tool. Examples are generating OrcaSlicer's calibration geometry and starting OrcaSlicer's slice action. Advice should stay a skill until there is a separately specified operation behind it that always behaves the same way.
76	
77	## Skills versus tools
78	
79	A skill is text the model reads. A tool is something the app executes. To decide which one a candidate is, ask one question: does it have to run, or does it only have to be read?
80	
81	- It has to run if it reads state the model does not have, computes something only OrcaSlicer can compute, or changes the project. That makes it a tool.
82	- It only has to be read if it is judgement, the order to do things in, facts about printing, how to interpret a tool's result, or which question to ask first. That makes it a skill.
83	
84	The section above covers tools. This section covers skills, and decides the cases that fall in between.
85	
86	A skill contains things the model could do by itself if it had the right knowledge. It contains nothing that executes. Examples:
87	
88	- judging evidence, such as telling an adhesion failure from wet filament in a photo;
89	- the order of a series of tool calls, and the reasons for that order. For "make it stronger": read the settings, change walls and infill, slice, read the report;
90	- facts about printing, such as what PETG tolerates;
91	- which question to ask when the answer would change the plan.
92	
93	A skill is a file on the Agent page, `AgentUI/src/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: frontmatter with its `name` and a `trigger`, a `description` or both, then the text the model gets. The page sends every skill once per connection with the `skills` bridge message. A skill with a trigger is the app's: when the event it names happens, the host adds it to the one request where the model first reads about the event, as the request's last item, and to no later request. A skill with a description is the model's: `skill_read` lists the described skills in its own description and returns one by name, and is offered only while at least one exists (none does yet). Four skills have triggers, one file each:
94	
95	- `file-loaded` (trigger `file_loaded`): the first message after a file is opened or imported is a judgement about the load report. It fires when the person opens or drops a file, after an in-app `object_import` (and a failed `project_open`) in the same turn, and in the opened project's chat after an in-app `project_open`, which replaces the conversation and so ends the turn that asked. An MCP client's loads fire nothing. The host sends a picture of the active plate with it and, when no purpose is recorded, one sentence of its own built from that state.
96	- `project-setup-changed` (trigger `setup_changed`): check the setup in force against the print's purpose. It fires on the result of an in-app `setup_record` that recorded a purpose for the first time or changed its fields (its result says which in `purposeChange`; a call that only restates the title to change the plan does not fire it), when the printer, filament, process or plate type differs from the setup the model was last asked to check under a recorded purpose (on the next tool result of the turn, or on the next turn's first request when the person changed it by hand), and on a turn's first request after the person restored an earlier version while a purpose is recorded. Each time the model is asked to check, the app saves the setup in force as the one checked. The model's own successful `printer_setup` fires nothing: the setup it chose is saved as checked at once (Kenneth, 2026-10-19), so the skill is for a setup that moved without the model, and a pairing its change breaks is caught by the slice-refusal facts and skill. It gives way to the file-loaded skill on a request that carries both, since that skill already asks for the same check.
97	- `slice-failed` (trigger `slice_failed`): a plate's last slice did not succeed, because OrcaSlicer's check refused the plate or the run failed. The adapter records why on the plate (`WorkspacePlate::slice_failure`: refused or failed, OrcaSlicer's words, the setting and object when named) at the moment it happens (a hook in `Plater::reslice`, `Workspace/SliceRequests.hpp`, and the run's completion event), worded by the print-issue monitor's `slice_failure_of`, and keeps it until the plate slices. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceFailure`; `slice_report` of an unsliced plate adds the check code and the object's name. The skill fires once per failure, on the first request that carries it: the result of the model's own `slice_start`, the turn the app starts when a slice the model started fails after its turn, or the next message after the person's Slice all. The same refusal again is the same failure.
98	- `print-issues` (trigger `print_issues`): what the print-issue chip's two buttons ask for and how to read what OrcaSlicer reports. The adapter reads a slice's warnings through the monitor's `slice_warnings_of` while the plate is active and keeps a summary on the plate while that slice is current (`WorkspacePlate::slice_warnings`: the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning, critical first, in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object). It counts every warning the chip lists, so the bed-temperature warning too, which `slice_report` leaves out. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceWarnings`. The skill fires on the request that carries a chip's message, and on the first request whose workspace shows warnings no request has carried yet, whether the person sliced (their next message) or the model did (the tool result that shows them, or the app's turn when its slice ended after its turn); a re-slice with the same warnings fires nothing.
99	
100	The cases in between:
101	
102	- **A procedure made of existing tool calls.** It is a skill for as long as carrying it out takes judgement. It becomes a tool only when the steps are fixed and the person wants the whole thing as one action that can be undone. If there are many such fixed sequences, they go in one workflow registry (see [When resources or skills are appropriate](#when-resources-or-skills-are-appropriate)).
103	- **An analysis.** It is a tool when OrcaSlicer computes it and always gets the same answer, such as overhang angles from geometry. It is a skill when it is a judgement about evidence. Pair that skill with the tool that supplies the evidence (`view_render`, `slice_report`).
104	- **Large reference data.** When the model needs only one part of the data, make it a tool that returns the part an argument selects, as `settings_search` does. When the model needs to see all of the data before it can use any of it, make it text. The printer list described under [Input design](#input-design) is the case we measured: putting the whole list in the instructions worked better than the search tool.
105	- **A tool description versus a skill.** A tool description says when to call that one tool, in the words a person would use. A skill says how several tools fit together and what to conclude from their results. If a tool description has grown into a step-by-step procedure, move the procedure out into a skill.
106	
107	When you are not sure, start with a skill. A skill is a text file that ships with the page. A tool costs the whole implementation sequence described below, including fakes, tests, and rebase evidence. Turn a skill into a tool only on the kind of evidence every tool starts from (see [Start with an eval failure](#start-with-an-eval-failure)). Either transcripts show the model getting the sequence wrong in ways that better text does not fix, or the action needs something only the app can give: all-or-nothing application, validation, or undo. The opposite sign exists too. If a skill has turned into exact values and calls in a fixed order, with no judgement between them, it should be written as a tool.
108	
109	How something gets loaded into the model's context does not decide whether it is a skill or a tool. Today a skill costs its one line in the instructions, and a tool costs its definition on the first request of a conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). If we later use the model platform's deferred loading, both will cost one index line plus a load when needed. A skill could then be a deferred read-only tool: the tool's description is the skill's index line, and the tool's result is the skill's text. Tools and skills would then be found the same way and covered by the same eval.

111	## Read, mutation, and destructive policy
112	
113	Decide what a tool may do from its action class in the registry, not from its name:
114	
115	- **Read-only:** cannot change the project, a preset, anything on disk, the printer, or any product state that is saved.
116	- **Mutation:** changes the project, a preset, or saved product state.
117	- **Destructive:** may delete, overwrite, discard, print, export, or restore history.
118	
119	The action class is information used for UI wording, MCP annotations, staleness checks, and the audit history. A valid tool call starts as soon as it has been validated. A tool that previews changes counts as read-only only if tests against both the fake and the real workspace adapter prove that it does none of these: make a preset dirty, raise the workspace revision, create history, cancel slicing, or write a file.
120	
121	## Asynchronous operations
122	
123	Make a tool asynchronous only when the real OrcaSlicer operation is asynchronous. Do not build a second engine for running jobs.
124	
125	Slicing, and any long-running action added later, works like this:
126	
127	1. The workspace command starts the work through its current OrcaSlicer owner and returns a stable action handle.
128	2. `ToolActivity` records that the action is running, and then its final state, with a limited amount of progress information.
129	3. When OrcaSlicer completes or fails, the workspace state advances or is invalidated.
130	4. After that event, the caller fetches the real slice report or the error.
131	5. Cancelling calls OrcaSlicer's real cancellation path, and reports whether the cancellation took effect before the work finished.
132	
133	MCP progress notifications are optional. They belong to one request and exist only to show progress. The progress value must never go backwards, and a client must always have another way to learn the final result. Add the MCP Tasks extension only when a real client or eval needs durable calls that outlive one request. An operation taking several seconds is not enough reason.
134	
135	The current coordinator runs an action in steps, on GUI ticks. It does not provide durable asynchronous jobs. The bridge accepts `notifications/cancelled` in both the legacy and the modern protocol versions. On receiving one, it closes the connection it was forwarding and suppresses any further output for that request. End of input (EOF) ends the bridge session. If the connection is lost before the final response, the client gets `connection_lost` with an **unknown outcome** warning. That is not proof that the mutation was cancelled. Never retry a mutation automatically after such a loss. Read the real state first.
136	
137	## Tool exposure
138	
139	By default, offer a tool through both adapters when both can supply the same inputs. Offer it through only one when the two sides get their context in different ways. The current cases:
140	
141	- `workspace_inspect` is offered through both adapters. Either side can then get the identity of a newly completed slice after slicing, without relying on the context it was given at the start of the turn.
142	- Import from an attachment (`object_import`) is in-app only, and import from a path (`object_import_file`) is MCP only. In the first case the file reaches the app through the conversation. In the second it arrives as an explicit path. These are two separate definitions that each say exactly what they do, both built on one workspace command. They are not one tool that behaves differently for different callers.
143	- `setup_record` is in-app only. The intent record and the pinned plan belong to the in-app chat. An external agent keeps what its user said, and its own plan, in its own conversation. MCP clients can still read both through `workspace_inspect` and `slice_report`. For the same reason, the in-app assistant's print guidance, which names these tools, is not part of the MCP server's instructions. That guidance is the "Intent and setup", "Preparation" and "Verification" paragraphs of the in-app prompt, written on the page in `AgentUI/src/projectInstructions.ts`.
144	- A future MCP diagnostics tool may be MCP only, if its purpose is to establish the external connection.
145	- The printer panel's five own tools carry only the `Printer` exposure. Neither adapter lists them. The panel's conversation offers all of them in every mode and refuses the calls that do not fit the conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). What the model reads back from one of these tools is the tool's own result. It is not wrapped in the host's workspace envelope.
146	
147	Write the reason for a restricted exposure next to the registry definition, and test it. Do not use exposure to make one tool behave differently for different callers. If two adapters need different behavior, either improve the shared command or create two separate definitions that each say what they really do.
148	
149	## When resources or skills are appropriate
150	
151	Do not make anything depend on MCP resources until the clients we intend to support have shown that their models fetch resources reliably. A tool that returns a size-limited amount of data is what every client can be expected to handle. Resources may be added as an optional second way to get data that is large, readable, and stable.
152	
153	Keep printing playbooks as skills the model can read (see [Skills versus tools](#skills-versus-tools)). Examples are reducing stringing, improving strength, and choosing a support strategy. Turn a workflow into an executable tool only when it corresponds to a named OrcaSlicer operation that always behaves the same way and has defined inputs, outputs, validation, and behavior for undo, reset, and cancellation. If many step-by-step workflows eventually qualify, build one workflow registry that the model can search, in preference to dozens of nearly identical tool definitions.

155	## Required implementation sequence for one new tool
156	
157	1. Add or update the failing eval and the expected transcript.
158	2. Find the real OrcaSlicer owner. Record how it behaves: object lifetimes, threading, undo history, and events.
159	3. Define the typed inputs, outputs, and errors of the workspace command.
160	4. Implement the command in the fake workspace adapter, and write the workspace contract tests.
161	5. Implement the command in the real workspace adapter, through the smallest possible seam in the owner.
162	6. Prove that making the edit directly in the GUI and making it through the tool leave the same observable state.
163	7. Add the registry definition, the decoder and validator, the link to the code that executes the tool, and the output schema.
164	8. Add coordinator tests for action class, staleness, all-or-nothing behavior, cancellation, and the final activity state.
165	9. Add projection tests for every adapter that offers the tool.
166	10. Add protocol fixtures and output-limit tests.
167	11. Run a harness against the real app, and record one end-to-end transcript with an external client.
168	12. Update the catalog below, and attach the verification and rebase evidence to the PR.
169	
170	Do not merge a registry entry that is backed only by the fake workspace.

## 2.11 Calibration and troubleshooting

This surface answers: **Is the printer-material combination behaving as expected?**

The audit found both guided calibration pages and more advanced generators.

### Relevant calibration capabilities

- Flow dynamics
- Flow rate
- Temperature
- Pressure advance
- Retraction
- Maximum volumetric speed
- VFA
- Junction deviation
- Input-shaping frequency and damping

### Why the agent cannot completely own calibration

Calibration depends on physical evidence:

- Filament may be wet.
- Adhesion may be poor.
- Transparent or reflective filament may confuse optical sensors.
- A nozzle may be worn or partially obstructed.
- A user may judge two samples differently.
- Automatic measurements contain uncertainty.
- An apparently better surface may reduce strength or accuracy elsewhere.

### What the agent should do

The agent should:

1. Diagnose the observed symptom.
2. Decide whether calibration is justified.
3. Select the appropriate test.
4. Choose safe test ranges.
5. Explain what to observe.
6. Analyze sensor data or photographs.
7. Recommend a result.
8. Say what was saved to the printer or filament profile and that it can be changed back.

The user should not be presented with every calibration parameter unless manual control is requested.

---

## 2.12 Privacy, updates, portability, and expert administration
## Writing UI code

Rules for anyone, human or agent, adding or changing a JusPrin surface. They
exist because every value that is typed by hand drifts from the design system and
from the other side of the app within weeks; today's guards catch most of it, but
only if the code goes through the token file in the first place.

1. **Never type a color, radius, font, or control size.** Every one comes
   from `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`. Native code reads it
   through `ShellTheme`: `palette(dark)` for color, `metrics()` for radii,
   spacing, and per-component sizes, `font(role)` for type. A stock
   `wxStaticText`, `wxTextCtrl`, or OrcaSlicer `Button` is
   dressed through `Shell/ShellRecipes.hpp`, never by calling its setters
   with literals. The Agent page uses only `var(--…)`: `--<group>-<name>` for
   color, `--radius-<name>`, `--font-<role>`, `--font-code`, and
   `--button-<recipe>-padding`.
2. **If the value you need has no token, add the token first.** Put it in
   the JSON, extend the guard in `tests/brand/test_brand_tokens.cpp` so a
   later edit cannot silently move it, then read it from code. Do not write
   the number "for now": the guards cannot see a literal that is already
   there, and the next reader cannot tell a decision from an accident. A
   value that exists in the design artifacts but not in the roles or scales is a design
   decision to raise, not a reason to type it.
3. **Layout spacing may stay literal, on the scale.** Padding between
   regions, gaps, and margins use 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, or 48 DIP.
   Control padding is not layout spacing; it comes from a button recipe.
4. **Pick the nearest role, never a bespoke size.** The roles are the whole
   type system. Bold at a body or label size is a role of its own; if a
   surface seems to need a size that no role has, see rule 2.
5. **The design system wins when it and the code disagree.** The two Claude
   artifacts are the source of truth (Kenneth, 2026-10-20; Figma is
   retired): the Design System
   (https://claude.ai/artifact/3zgiix8rAw3rXextQnR5UL) and the "JusPrin v2"
   canvas (https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v). Change the
   token file to match, or, when the code's value is the one to keep, change
   the artifact first. Do not trust old commit messages about either.
6. **Run the guards before calling UI work done:** `brand_tokens_tests`,
   `shell_theme_tests`, and `npm test` in `AgentUI`. Then look at the surface
   in the running app; the guards prove the code went through the tokens,
   not that the result looks right.
7. **Upstream files are off limits for style.** OrcaSlicer's own screens are
   retinted through the hooks `BrandPalette.cpp` installs and nothing else;
   see [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md). Their radii and fonts stay
   OrcaSlicer's until the surface is replaced.
